title: Of glory
paragraphs: There is the name, and there is the thing. The name is a sound that denotes and signifies the thing; the name is no part of the thing or of its substance — it is a foreign piece attached to the thing, on the outside. God, who is all fullness in Himself and the height of all perfection, cannot grow or add anything to Himself within; but His name can be magnified and increased by the blessing and praise we attach to His outward works. That praise, since we cannot incorporate it into Him (He being incapable of any further good), we attach to His name, which is the part of Him nearest to us. So glory and honour belong to God alone, and nothing is more contrary to reason than to chase after them for ourselves: poor and needy within, our essence being imperfect and in constant need of improvement, that is where we ought to direct all our effort. We are hollow and empty; it is not with wind and voice that we are to fill ourselves; we need more solid substance to repair us. A man starving with hunger would be very simple to seek a gay garment before a good meal: we are to look after what we most need. As our ordinary prayer puts it:
"Gloria in excelsis Deo, et in terra pax hominibus."

We lack beauty, health, wisdom, virtue, and the other essential qualities; outward ornaments should be looked after only when the necessities are provided for. Theology treats this subject amply and far more fittingly than I can, but I am not much versed in it.

Chrysippus and Diogenes were the earliest and most committed advocates of contempt for glory; they argued that of all pleasures none is more dangerous, none more to be avoided, than the pleasure that comes from the approval of others. And experience does in fact show us many hurtful treacheries in it. Nothing poisons princes so much as flattery, and nothing makes it easier for the wicked to gain credit and favour with them; no procuring is so apt and so commonly used to corrupt the chastity of women as flattering them with praise of themselves. The first charm the Sirens used to lure Ulysses is of this kind:
"Deca vers nous, deca, o tres-louable Ulysse, Et le plus grand honneur don't la Grece fleurisse."
["Come over to us, come, much-praised Ulysses, greatest ornament and pride of Greece." — Homer, Odyssey, xii. 184.]
These philosophers said that all the glory in the world was not worth a man of sense lifting a finger to obtain:
"Gloria quantalibet quid erit, si gloria tantum est?"
["What is glory, however glorious, if it is only glory?" — Juvenal, Sat., vii. 81.]

I say this of glory taken on its own; for it often brings other goods along with it that are quite reasonably wanted. It earns us goodwill and makes us less exposed to insults and slights from others, and so on. It was also one of the main doctrines of Epicurus: his sect's precept, Conceal your life, which forbids encumbering oneself with public business and office, presupposes contempt for glory — the world's approval of the actions we perform in public. Anyone who tells us to hide ourselves, to have no concern but for ourselves, who would not have us known to others, would still less have us honoured and praised; and so he advises Idomeneus not to regulate his actions by common opinion at all, except so far as needed to avoid the practical inconveniences that the contempt of men might bring upon him.

These arguments are, in my view, very sound and reasonable; but we are, I don't quite know how, double in ourselves, which is why we don't believe what we believe and cannot disengage from what we condemn. Look at the last words of Epicurus, dying: they are grand and worthy of such a philosopher, and yet they contain some hint of self-commendation and of that very humour he had spent his life denouncing. Here is the letter he dictated just before his last gasp:
"EPICURUS TO HERMACHUS, health.

"As I am passing the happy and last day of my life, I write this — at the same time afflicted by such pain in my bladder and bowels that nothing could be greater, but it was repaid by the pleasure that the memory of my discoveries and doctrines brought to my soul. Now, as the affection you have always borne, from your infancy, towards me and philosophy demands, take on the protection of Metrodorus's children."

That is the letter. And the reason I interpret his "pleasure of soul concerning his discoveries" as carrying a reference to the reputation he hoped to leave behind is the form of his will: in it he orders Amynomachus and Timocrates, his heirs, to defray every January the costs of celebrating his birthday as Hermachus should direct, and the expense of entertaining the philosophers, his friends, on the twentieth of each moon, who should assemble in honour of his memory and of Metrodorus.

Carneades took the opposite view: he held that glory was to be desired for its own sake, just as we love our posthumous descendants for their own sake, even though we will have no knowledge or enjoyment of them. This opinion has not failed to be the more widely followed, as is usually the case with views that fit our inclinations. Aristotle gives glory first place among external goods, and avoids as extreme vices either the immoderate pursuit or the immoderate avoidance of it. I think that if we still had the books Cicero wrote on this subject, we should find pretty stories there, for he was so possessed by this passion that, if he had dared, I think he could happily have gone the whole way the others went — saying that virtue itself is not to be valued except for the honour that always attends it:
"Paulum sepultae distat inertiae Celata virtus:"
["Virtue concealed differs little from dead sloth." — Horace, Od., iv. 9, 29.]
An opinion so false that I am sorry it could ever enter the mind of a man who was honoured with the name of philosopher.

If this were true, men need only be virtuous in public; we would have no further reason to keep the operations of the soul — the true seat of virtue — regular and in order, except insofar as they come to the knowledge of others. Is it then a matter only of slyly and circumspectly doing wrong? "If you knew," says Carneades, "of a serpent lurking in a place where, with no warning, someone is about to sit down, by whose death you stood to gain, you do wrong if you do not warn him of the danger; and so much the more because the act would be known to no one but you." If we do not take the rule of right-doing from ourselves, if impunity passes with us for justice, to how many kinds of wickedness will we abandon ourselves every day? I do not find what Sextus Peduceus did — faithfully returning the treasure that C. Plotius had committed to his sole secrecy and trust (a thing I have often done myself) — so very commendable; I should have thought doing otherwise an execrable baseness. And I think it useful in our day to recall the example of P. Sextilius Rufus, whom Cicero accuses of having entered upon an inheritance against his conscience, though not against the law — indeed by the law's own determination; and of M. Crassus and Hortensius, who, because of their authority and power, were called in by a stranger to share in a forged will (so that he could secure his own part), and were content not to have a hand in the forgery while not refusing to take their share. Safe enough, if they could shelter themselves from accusations, witnesses, and the law's notice:
"Meminerint Deum se habere testem, id est (ut ego arbitror) mentem suam."
["Let them remember they have God as witness — that is (as I interpret it), their own conscience." — Cicero, De Offic., iii. 10.]

Virtue is a very vain and frivolous thing if it derives its standing from glory; and it is no use trying to give it a station of its own, separate from fortune — for what is more accidental than reputation?
"Profecto fortuna in omni re dominatur: ea res cunctas ex libidine magis, quam ex vero, celebrat, obscuratque."
["Fortune rules in everything; it celebrates or obscures things more out of its own caprice than out of truth." — Sallust, Catilina, c. 8.]

Arranging it so that one's actions are known and seen is purely the work of fortune; it is chance that hands us glory, according to its own whim. I have often seen her go before merit, and often far outstrip it. Whoever first compared glory to a shadow knew better than he realised: both are eminently empty things. Glory, like a shadow, sometimes goes before the body and sometimes stretches out far beyond it. Those who instruct gentlemen to use their courage only for the sake of honour:
"Quasi non sit honestum, quod nobilitatum non sit;"
["As if a thing were not virtuous unless it were famous." — Cicero, De Offic., iii. 10.]

what do they teach but never to risk anything unobserved, and to check carefully whether there are witnesses present to bring back the news of their courage? Yet a thousand occasions for good action arise that cannot be noticed. How many brave individual acts are buried in the crowd of a battle? Anyone who takes it on himself to watch another's conduct in such confusion is not very busy fighting himself, and the testimony he gives of his comrades' behaviour is evidence against his own:
"Vera et sapiens animi magnitudo, honestum illud, quod maxime naturam sequitur, in factis positum, non in gloria, judicat."
["True and wise greatness of soul judges that bravery, which most follows nature, consists in deeds rather than in glory." — Cicero, De Offic., i. 19.]

All the glory I claim from my life is that I have lived it quietly — quietly, not according to Metrodorus, or Arcesilaus, or Aristippus, but according to myself. Since philosophy has not found any road to tranquillity that works for everyone in common, let each man look for it on his own.

What do Caesar and Alexander owe the boundless grandeur of their reputations to but fortune? How many men has she snuffed out at the start of their progress, of whom we know nothing, who brought as much courage to the task as they did, if bad luck had not cut them off in their first sortie? Among so many great dangers I do not remember reading anywhere that Caesar was ever wounded; a thousand men have fallen in less dangerous moments than the least of those he went through. An infinite number of brave actions must be performed without witness and lost before one of them counts for anything. A man is not always on top of a breach or at the head of an army, in his general's sight, as if on a stage. He is often surprised between the hedge and the ditch; he has to risk his life over a chicken coop; he has to dislodge four ragged musketeers from a barn; he has to spur out alone from his troop and attempt something solo, as necessity demands. And anyone who watches will find, I believe, that the least glamorous occasions are always the most dangerous, and that in the wars of our own time more good men have been lost on small occasions, in some dispute over a paltry little fort, than in places of great importance where their courage could have been honourably employed.

The man who thinks his death was wasted unless it falls on some signal occasion, instead of illustrating his death, deliberately obscures his life, letting many perfectly fitting occasions for risking himself slip through his hands; and every fitting one is illustrious enough — every man's conscience is sufficient trumpet to him.
"Gloria nostra est testimonium conscientiae nostrae."
["Our glory is the testimony of our conscience." — Corinthians, i. 1.]

The man who is good only that he may be seen to be good, that he may be the better esteemed once it is known, who will only do well on condition that his virtue is known to men — that is a man from whom not much service is to be expected:

"Credo ch'el reste di quel verno, cose Facesse degne di tener ne conto; Ma fur fin'a quel tempo si nascose, Che non a colpa mia s'hor non le conto Perche Orlando a far l'opre virtuose Piu ch'a narrar le poi sempre era pronto; Ne mai fu alcun' de'suoi fatti espresso, Se non quando ebbe i testimonii appresso."

["The rest of the winter, I believe, was spent in deeds worthy of being recounted; but they were so concealed at the time that it is no fault of mine if I cannot tell them now, for Orlando was always more eager to do brave deeds than to narrate them, and none of his actions were ever made known except those that had witnesses present." — Ariosto, Orlando Furioso, xi. 81.]

A man must go to war out of duty, and expect the reward that never fails brave and worthy actions, however private — or even virtuous thoughts: the satisfaction a well-set conscience feels in itself when it acts well. A man must be valiant for his own sake, for the advantage of having his courage lodged in a firm and secure place against the assaults of fortune:
"Virtus, repulsae nescia sordidae, Intaminatis fulget honoribus, Nec sumit, aut ponit secures Arbitrio popularis aurae."
["Virtue, knowing no base rebuff, shines in untainted honours, and neither takes nor lays down dignities at the mere caprice of the popular breeze." — Horace, Od., iii. 2, 17.]

It is not for outward show that the soul has to play its part, but for ourselves inside, where no eyes can pierce but our own; there she defends us from the fear of death, of pain, of shame itself; there she arms us against the loss of our children, our friends, and our fortunes; and when the chance offers, she leads us into the hazards of war:
"Non emolumento aliquo, sed ipsius honestatis decore."
["Not for any profit, but for the honour of honesty itself." — Cicero, De Finib., i. 10.]
This profit is far greater, and far more worth wanting and hoping for, than honour and glory, which are nothing but a favourable judgment passed on us.

A dozen men have to be called out of a whole nation to judge a question of an acre of land; and the judgment of our inclinations and our actions — the most difficult and most important matter there is — we refer to the voice and verdict of the crowd, mother of ignorance, injustice, and inconstancy. Is it reasonable that a wise man's life should depend on the judgment of fools?
"An quidquam stultius, quam, quos singulos contemnas, eos aliquid putare esse universos?"
["Can anything be more foolish than to think that those you despise one by one amount to something taken all together?" — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., v. 36.]
Whoever makes it his business to please them will have plenty to do and never be done; it is a target that can never be aimed at, let alone hit:
"Nil tam inaestimabile est, quam animi multitudinis."
["Nothing is so impossible to gauge as the minds of the multitude." — Livy, xxxi. 34.]
Demetrius said pleasantly of the voice of the people that he made no more account of what came from above than of what came from below. Cicero says more:
"Ego hoc judico, si quando turpe non sit, tamen non esse non turpe, quum id a multitudine laudatur."
["My view is that even if a thing is not foul in itself, it nevertheless cannot help becoming so when commended by the multitude." — Cicero, De Finib., ii. 15.]

No art, no exercise of wit, could steer our steps so as to follow so wandering and irregular a guide. In this windy confusion of vulgar rumours and opinions pushing us around, no path worth anything can be chosen. Let us not set ourselves so floating and shifting a goal; let us follow reason steadily; let public approval follow us along if it likes, and since it depends entirely on fortune, we have no more reason to expect it by any other route than that. Even if I were not inclined to follow the right road because it is right, I would still follow it, having found by experience that, at the end of the reckoning, it is usually the happiest and the most useful.
"Dedit hoc providentia hominibus munus, ut honesta magis juvarent."
["Providence has given men this gift, that honourable things are also the most pleasing." — Quintilian, Inst. Orat., i. 12.]

The old mariner said this to Neptune in a great tempest: "O God, you will save me if you will, and if you choose you will destroy me; but whatever happens, I will hold my rudder straight." I have seen in my time a thousand pliant, half-bred, ambiguous men — none of whom anyone doubted was more worldly-wise than I — lose themselves, where I have saved myself:
"Risi successus posse carere dolos."
["I have laughed to see cunning fail of its success." — Ovid, Heroid., i. 18.]

Paulus Aemilius, setting out on his glorious expedition to Macedonia, charged the people of Rome above all things not to talk about his actions during his absence. The licence of opinions is a great disturbance to great affairs; not everyone has Fabius's firmness against common, hostile, and unjust tongues — he preferred to let his authority be carved up by the vain fancies of men rather than perform his charge less well in order to keep a favourable reputation and the people's applause.
There is some natural sweetness, I don't know what, in hearing oneself praised — but we are far too fond of it:
"Laudari metuam, neque enim mihi cornea fibra est; Sed recti finemque extremumque esse recuso Euge tuum, et belle."
["I would fear to be praised — my heart is not made of horn — but I refuse to admit that 'Excellent! Beautifully done!' are the proper aim and end of virtue." — Persius, i. 47.]

I care not so much what I am in others' opinion as what I am in my own; I would be rich on my own account, not by borrowing. Strangers see only events and outward appearances; anyone can put a good face on it when their insides are trembling with terror — they do not see my heart, they see my face. People are right to deplore the hypocrisy that is in war, for what is easier for an old soldier than to dodge in moments of danger and counterfeit bravery when he has no more heart than a chicken? There are so many ways to avoid putting one's person at risk that we have deceived the world a thousand times before we are actually committed to real danger; and even then, finding ourselves under an unavoidable need to do something, we manage for that moment to hide our fears by putting on a good face, though our hearts pound. Whoever had Plato's ring, which makes whoever wears it invisible when turned palm-inward, would find that a great many people would often hide themselves when they ought most to appear, and would regret being placed in so honourable a post where necessity forces them to be bold.
"Falsus honor juvat, et mendax infamia terret Quem nisi mendosum et mendacem?"
["False honour pleases, lying infamy terrifies — whom else but the guilty and the sickened?" — Horace, Ep., i. 16, 89.]

So we see how all judgments founded on outward appearances are extraordinarily uncertain and questionable, and that there is no surer testimony than each man's to himself. In these things, how many soldiers' boys are companions of our glory? The man who holds steady in an open trench — what is he doing more than the fifty poor sappers who clear the way for him and cover it with their own bodies for fivepence a day?
"Non quicquid turbida Roma Elevet, accedas; examenque improbum in illa Castiges trutina: nec te quaesiveris extra."
["Do not assent if turbulent Rome disparages something; do not correct a false balance by that scale; do not seek yourself outside yourself." — Persius, Sat., i. 5.]

Spreading our names through many mouths is what we call making them great; we want them well received there, and want this circulation to redound to their advantage — which is the only excusable element in the design. But the excess of this disease goes so far that many want a name no matter what kind. Trogus Pompeius says of Herostratus, and Livy of Manlius Capitolinus, that they were more ambitious for a great reputation than for a good one. Very common — we are more anxious that men should speak of us than how they speak of us; it is enough for us that our names are often mentioned, in whatever manner. It looks as though to be known is in some sense to have one's life and its duration held in others' keeping. I, for my part, hold that I exist only in myself; and as for that other life of mine that lies in the knowledge of my friends — considered nakedly and simply in itself — I know perfectly well that I feel no pleasure or enjoyment from it except through the vanity of a fantastic opinion; and once I am dead, I shall feel it still less, and shall meanwhile lose any real advantages that sometimes accidentally follow from it.

I shall have no more handle by which to grasp reputation, nor any by which reputation can grasp me; to expect my name to be advanced by it — in the first place, I have no name properly my own. Of the two I have, one is shared by my whole family, and indeed by others as well: there are two families in Paris and Montpellier whose surname is Montaigne, another in Brittany, and one in Xaintonge, De La Montaigne. The shifting of a single syllable would be enough to tangle our affairs, and I shall share their glory while perhaps they share my discredit; and besides, my ancestors used to be surnamed Eyquem, a name a family well known in England today still bears. As to my other name, anyone may take it who likes, and so I might end up doing honour to a porter in my own stead. And even if I had a distinction all my own, what is there to distinguish, when I am no more? Can it point out and favour nothingness?
"Non levior cippus nunc imprimit ossa? Laudat posteritas! Nunc non e manibus illis, Nunc non a tumulo fortunataque favilla, Nascentur violae?"
["Does the tomb press less heavily on my bones? Does posterity praise me? Not from my shade, not from my tomb, not from the lucky ash will violets grow." — Persius, Sat., i. 37.]

I have spoken of this elsewhere. As for the rest: in a great battle where ten thousand men are maimed or killed, there are not fifteen who get noticed; it must take some real eminence, or some consequence of great importance that fortune adds to it, to make a private action stand out — not just of a musketeer, but even of a great captain. To kill a man, or two, or ten; to expose yourself bravely to the worst peril of death — that is indeed something for each of us, since we risk everything; but from the world's perspective they are things so ordinary, and so many of them are seen every day, and there must be so many of the same kind in succession to produce any notable effect, that we cannot expect any particular fame from it:
"Casus multis hic cognitus, ac jam Tritus, et a medio fortunae ductus acervo."
["The accident is known to many, and now stale; drawn from the middle of fortune's heap." — Juvenal, Sat., xiii. 9.]

Of the many thousands of brave men who have died sword in hand in France in the last fifteen hundred years, not a hundred have come to our knowledge. The memory not just of the commanders, but of the battles and victories themselves, is buried and gone; the fortunes of more than half the world, for want of any record, do not stir from their place and vanish without leaving any duration. If I had unknown events in my possession, I think I could easily outdo what is recorded, in every kind of example. Is it not strange that even of the Greeks and Romans, with all their writers and witnesses, with so many rare and noble exploits, so few have come down to us?
"Ad nos vix tenuis famae perlabitur aura."
["To us scarcely a thin rumour drifts down." — Aeneid, vii. 646.]

It will be a great thing if, a hundred years from now, it is remembered in general that in our day there were civil wars in France. The Lacedaemonians, before going into battle, sacrificed to the Muses, so that their actions might be well and worthily written up; they regarded it as a divine and uncommon favour that brave deeds should find witnesses able to give them life and memory. Do we expect that at every musket-shot we take, at every danger we run, there should be a clerk standing by to record it? And besides, a hundred clerks may write them down whose commentaries will last no longer than three days and never come to anyone's eye. We do not have a thousandth part of the ancient writings; it is fortune that gives them a shorter or longer life, according to her favour, and one may reasonably doubt whether what we have is not the worst — never having seen the rest. People do not write histories of trivial matters: you must have been a general in the conquest of an empire or a kingdom, you must have won fifty-two pitched battles, always with the smaller army, as Caesar did. Ten thousand brave men and many great captains lost their lives valiantly in his service whose names lasted no longer than their wives and children lived:
"Quos fama obscura recondit."
["Whom an obscure reputation conceals." — Aeneid, v. 302.]

Even those whom we see acquit themselves well — three months or three years after they are gone, no more is said of them than if they had never lived. Anyone who considers fairly, and in due proportion, what kind of men and what kind of actions sustain glory in the records of history will find that very few actions and very few persons of our time have any rightful claim there. How many worthy men have we known who outlived their own reputation, who saw and endured the honour and glory most justly earned in their youth extinguished in their very presence? And for three years of this fantastic, imaginary life, we are to throw away our true and essential life, and pledge ourselves to a perpetual death! The wise propose a nobler and juster end in so important an enterprise:
"Recte facti, fecisse merces est: officii fructus, ipsum officium est."
["The reward of doing well is to have done it; the fruit of a service is the service itself." — Seneca, Ep., 8.]

It might be excusable in a painter or another craftsman, or in a rhetorician or grammarian, to try to make himself a name through his works; but acts of virtue are too noble in themselves to seek any reward other than their own value — and certainly not in the vanity of human judgments.

If, however, this false opinion is so useful to the public that it keeps men in their duty; if the people are stirred up by it to virtue; if princes are moved to see the world bless the memory of Trajan and curse that of Nero; if it strikes them to see the name of that great brute, once so terrible and dreaded, freely cursed and reviled by every schoolboy — then by all means let it grow, and be nursed and cherished among us as much as possible. Plato too, bending his whole effort towards making his citizens virtuous, advises them not to despise the people's good opinion and esteem, and says it happens, by a certain divine inspiration, that even the wicked, in word and opinion alike, can rightly distinguish the virtuous from the wicked. Plato and his master are both remarkable, bold artificers in adding divine operations and revelations wherever human force runs out:
"Ut tragici poetae confugiunt ad deum, cum explicare argumenti exitum non possunt:"
["As the tragic poets fly to some god when they cannot work out the resolution of the plot." — Cicero, De Nat. Deor., i. 20.]

It was perhaps for this reason that Timon, mocking him, called him the great manufacturer of miracles. Since men, by their inadequacy, cannot pay themselves enough in real coin, let counterfeit be added on top. It is a method all legislators have used; there is no government that does not have some mixture either of ceremonial pomp or of false belief, serving as a curb to keep the people in their duty. That is why most of them have fabulous origins, enriched with supernatural mysteries — and why bastard religions have gained credit and been countenanced by men of understanding. It is why Numa and Sertorius, to give their men a better opinion of them, fed them this foolery: one claimed that the nymph Egeria, the other that his white hind, brought him all his counsels from the gods. The authority Numa gave to his laws under the patronage of this goddess, Zoroaster, lawgiver of the Bactrians and Persians, gave to his under the name of the god Oromasdes; Trismegistus, lawgiver of the Egyptians, under that of Mercury; Zamolxis, lawgiver of the Scythians, under that of Vesta; Charondas, lawgiver of the Chalcidians, under that of Saturn; Minos, lawgiver of the Cretans, under that of Jupiter; Lycurgus, lawgiver of the Spartans, under that of Apollo; and Draco and Solon, lawgivers of the Athenians, under that of Minerva. And every government has a god at the head of it — the others falsely, that one truly, which Moses set over the Jews at their departure out of Egypt. The religion of the Bedouins, as the Sire de Joinville reports, among other things enjoined a belief that the soul of one of them who died for his prince passed into another body, happier, more beautiful, and stronger than the former — by which they much more readily ventured their lives:
"In ferrum mens prona viris, animaeque capaces Mortis, et ignavum est rediturae parcere vitae."
["Their minds are eager for the sword, their souls capable of death; it is cowardly to spare a life that will be renewed." — Lucan, i. 461.]
A very comforting belief, however mistaken. Every nation has many such examples of its own; but the subject would require a treatise of its own.
To add a word to what has gone before, I would advise the ladies no longer to call by the name of honour what is merely their duty:
"Ut enim consuetudo loquitur, id solum dicitur honestum, quod est populari fama gloriosum;"
["As custom puts it, that alone is called honest which is glorious in public report." — Cicero, De Finibus, ii. 15.]

Their duty is the target; their honour is only the outer rind. Nor would I have them give this excuse as their reason for refusing — I assume that their intentions, their desires, and their wills (things in which their honour is not at all involved, since nothing of them appears outwardly) are much better regulated than the acts:
"Quae quia non liceat, non facit, illa facit:"
["She who only refuses because it is forbidden, consents." — Ovid, Amor., iii. 4, 4.]

The offence, before God and in the conscience, would be as great in the desire as in the deed; and besides, the acts are so private and secret in themselves that they could easily be kept from the knowledge of others — in which the honour consists — were it not for some other respect to their duty, and the affection they bear for chastity in itself. A woman of honour will far rather lose her honour than wound her conscience.
